doc.title: Jay Leonhart interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 15, 1998 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Whether musicians need to be high to play
summary: He discusses the belief that musicians play better drunk or high and why he thinks sobriety is better for the work.

story.theme_name: Drink, drugs and the bandstand's casualties
story.community_name: Drugs and drink on the bandstand and the road

blocks.x: You know besides the fact that you’re in night clubs so much, and that you’re around booze, do you think that there’s an attitude with some musicians that you kind of need to be high, on some substance or other, to play jazz?

Yeah. Sure. I mean I know guys, very good musicians who at times in their lives really felt that they played much better drunk, high, whatever. And I understand that. I understand that. But it’s hard to last like that. It’s very tough on your system. And drinking is a perilous thing because it really takes it out of you. And you have that one little drink and just that one little drink, and you’re in the club and somebody wants to buy you another and you say, oh, no, I’ve had my drink. Oh, no, no. Of course you’re going to have a drink. Sure, sure, sure. Well what’s another night down the drain. And if you’re really serious about it, it’s like an astronomer. He’s going to go up and look at the stars — let’s have a few drinks first. Really you want to see the stars, you want to see, you want to be able to look. If you’re an astronomer, you don’t want to be drunk, you want to really look at what you’re doing. Well with playing music, hopefully it might be the same thing. And for me it has been for the last thirty years. And I don’t mean to be preachy about it, but, okay.
